brand_fidelity.evidence: Harbour #1F3A4D anchors the header, headings and amounts, and Signal #C2462B is used sparingly for the header rule and primary buttons. The warm paper (#F5F2EA) and card (#FFFDF8) neutrals make it feel steady rather than bank-like, and Fraunces with Figtree suits a trustworthy, quietly confident tool. The Settle up hint 'Owing each other is normal' states the principle directly. However, colouring every 'owes' amount and bar in red against green 'is owed' slightly frames debt as a warning.

visual_craft.evidence: Hierarchy is clear: eyebrow, Fraunces h2, muted hint, then content, on a consistent 20–24px card gap and a 5fr/6fr grid that stacks cleanly at 390px. The weak spot is the expense list. Each row stacks description, meta, a bare 'Shares' label and a right-aligned Remove button on its own line, so three expenses take far more height than the information needs on both widths.

copy_voice.evidence: Strings are plain and specific. Examples: 'Shared trip costs, settled plainly.', 'What was it for?', '“Ana” is already on the trip.', 'Use a positive amount with at most two decimal places, like 42.50.' and 'Saved in this browser only. Nothing leaves your device.' Buttons are verbs and empty states tell you what to do next. Eyebrows like 'Log it' and 'The record' are a touch cute, and every card repeats eyebrow, title and hint even when the hint is redundant ('Newest first.').

ux_completeness.evidence: All brief states are handled. That covers distinct empty messages per section, per-field errors with aria-invalid and focus moved to the offending field, and typed values kept on error. It also covers aria-live announcements after actions, a confirm before 'Start a new trip', and removal only for people with no expenses ('In expenses' tag otherwise). Balances read well with a centred zero scale, and settle-up rows are easy to act on. The 'Shares' disclosure has its marker removed via display:inline-block, so it doesn't look clickable.

code_quality.evidence: State is cleanly separated into load/save/render, and load() validates stored data defensively. Amounts are parsed with a strict regex into integer cents, and shares() distributes remainder cents in trip order. settle() is a greedy matcher that guarantees at most n−1 transfers. Output is HTML-escaped throughout, semantics are sound (fieldset/legend for the split, labels on every input, details/summary, sr-only live region), and focus handling after delete and reset is considered.

directed_design.evidence: There are specific, brand-led choices: a custom keel/balance SVG mark with a Signal pivot dot, a Signal rule under the navy header, and balance bars that tip left or right of a centre line, which literally expresses 'even keel'. Tabular numerals are used on money. Template habits remain: an uppercase eyebrow on every card, pill chips and tags, and uniform cards for every section.

ai_tells: Uppercase letter-spaced eyebrow above every single card heading ('THE GROUP', 'LOG IT', 'WHERE THINGS STAND', 'WHO PAYS WHOM', 'THE RECORD')
Every section wrapped in an identical rounded bordered card
brand_violations: Red (signal-ink) text and red bars for every person who 'owes', paired with green for 'is owed', leans on a warning colour code that frames owing as a problem, against 'Owing money between friends is normal'
review.best_detail: The balance scale, with a fixed centre tick and bars tipping left in Signal or right in green, makes 'getting back to even' visible at a glance and ties the data display directly to the Even Keel name.
review.worst_detail: Each expense row carries an unmarked 'Shares' summary that looks like a stray label, plus a Remove button on its own line, which bloats the list and hides the per-person breakdown behind a control users won't recognise.
